splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in withdrawal liability calculations.

circuits.name: D.C. Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled when the supervisee absconds, so the clock stops running and the court retains jurisdiction to revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the term expires as specified in the judgment regardless of the supervisee's compliance.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1)—which categorically bars claims previously presented—when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If it applies, federal prisoners are barred from re-raising any previously presented claim; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a stricter gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s own requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution affects whether candidates can challenge rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices before an election takes place, or whether such disputes must wait until after the election.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when a state law allegedly dilutes lawful votes or changes election procedures in ways that affect the candidate's chances.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's alleged competitive injury from a ballot-counting law is too speculative and generalized to satisfy Article III standing requirements.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps judicial deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity should prevail over deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary when interpreting ambiguous sentencing guidelines provisions in criminal cases. The Third Circuit held that deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity takes priority. The issue has gained significance after the Supreme Court's decisions in Kisor v. Wilkie and Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations in criminal contexts, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive guidance.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that deference to the Sentencing Commission's authoritative commentary takes priority over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous guidelines provisions, even in criminal sentencing contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text itself does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson, or whether it impermissibly expands the unambiguous guideline text. The Seventh Circuit defers to the commentary, while multiple other circuits have rejected it.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and other inchoate offenses in the definition of 'controlled substance offense' is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline entitled to controlling weight under Stinson.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 cannot expand the definition beyond the plain text, especially after Kisor v. Wilkie narrowed the scope of deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether 'and' means 'and' or 'or' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits hold that defendants are disqualified only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits hold that possessing any one is disqualifying. The split creates geographic sentencing disparities for defendants with identical criminal histories.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if the defendant meets all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' distributively or disjunctively.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state controls a substance not listed on the federal schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) requires the underlying substance to be controlled under federal law or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require the substance to be federally controlled. The issue affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state schedules suffice
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law regardless of whether the substance is controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Federal schedules required
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also controlled under federal law, grafting a federal-law limitation onto the guideline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can serve as a basis for compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit in Crandall and the Seventh Circuit in Thacker held that such changes cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while other circuits have allowed non-retroactive legal changes to be considered. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this by permitting such reductions, but the Seventh Circuit found this exceeded the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction, and that the Sentencing Commission's policy statement allowing such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons warranting a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when revoking and resentencing, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust and public safety considerations.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis permits district courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split. Other circuits limit the purpose of revocation sentences to addressing the breach of the court's trust and protecting public safety, rather than punishing the underlying violating conduct.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly consider punishment for the violation conduct when imposing a sentence upon revocation of supervised release.

positions.label: Revocation sentence should focus on breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that the primary purpose of a revocation sentence is to sanction the breach of the court's trust inherent in the violation, not to punish the defendant for the underlying violating conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or the debtor under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A). The Ninth Circuit holds that such appreciation inures to the estate, while other circuits have concluded that it belongs to the debtor. The issue significantly affects debtors' incentives to convert and the distribution to creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with the broad scope of § 541(a), means that post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and § 348(f)(1)(A)'s purpose of protecting good-faith converting debtors means that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner's challenge to BOP decisions regarding conditions or terms of confinement (such as transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act) must be brought as a habeas corpus petition or may be brought as a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions and terms of confinement that do not directly contest the fact or duration of imprisonment must be brought via habeas corpus or may proceed as civil rights claims. The Eighth Circuit acknowledges this unresolved conflict spanning more than half a century, which affects how federal prisoners challenge BOP decisions on transfers, halfway house placements, and earned time credits under the First Step Act.

positions.label: Habeas is available for conditions/terms challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 is available to challenge BOP decisions about the execution of a sentence, including transfer to prerelease custody and application of First Step Act time credits.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons

positions.label: Habeas is not available; civil rights action required
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement that do not affect the fact or duration of imprisonment are not cognizable in habeas and must instead be brought through civil rights statutes such as Bivens.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal of a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order in a criminal case is governed by the civil appeal deadline (60 days) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment—which permits criminal defendants to recover fees from the government for frivolous, vexatious, or bad-faith prosecutions—is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of the appellate deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, noting a lopsided circuit split on the issue.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 60-day appeal deadline for civil cases under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter 14-day appeal deadline for criminal cases under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Other circuits have taken varying approaches to the collateral order doctrine's application to sealing orders, with some limiting immediate appealability to narrower categories of sealed materials.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses involves a value of high order that is effectively unreviewable on appeal from final judgment, satisfying the collateral order doctrine.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are generally not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated through other means, including post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied differing standards for evaluating discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, leading to inconsistent results regarding liability and available remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, which impacts hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more expansive standard for discrimination claims against business operators, allowing broader theories of liability and remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard that limits the scope of actionable discrimination claims and available remedies against business operators.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
